subject: Shipwright pilot: ops constraints, SLO targets & next steps

Subject: Shipwright pilot: ops constraints, SLO targets & next steps

Alex / Priya — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our side and proposed next steps so we have a single source of truth.

Top pain points you shared
- Peak label-generation bursts during end-of-day batch runs cause queued requests and 95/99p latency spikes.
- Tight SLAs for customer confirmation: ~100–200 real-time calls/sec at 95th < 80–120ms is the target.
- Data locality / privacy: production traffic must stay in your AWS account/network and meet SOC2 controls.

What we heard as success metrics
- Functional: accurate, structured label output (JSON) and deterministic post-processing on Redwood outputs.
- Performance: 99th percentile latency under 200ms for single-turn generation at 2k tokens per minute aggregate, with 95p under 120ms for short payloads (~128 tokens).
- Cost target: keep per-label inference cost below $0.004 on average.

Technical notes & initial recommendations (high level)
- Model: start with a 3B-class open model quantized to 4-bit for latency/cost tradeoffs; fallback to a 7B for complex invoices.
- Serving: Dedicated pool (reserved capacity) in your VPC using Redwood Private. This gives predictable throughput and keeps traffic in your network.
- Caching & batching: deploy KV prefix caching for common templates + small continuous batching window (5–10ms) to smooth bursts without adding >20ms p99 latency.
- Fallback policy: route to a higher-capacity instance group for tail-latency events; automated model variant fallback in the router.

Proposed next steps
1) We’ll share a sizing sheet and a short SLO proposal (attached). Please confirm the sample traffic profile (peak qps, average tokens per request) and any retention/PII constraints.
2) Schedule a short infra sync (30m) with your platform team — we proposed Wed 10/07 or Thu 10/08.
3) Run a 1-week pilot: Redwood provides a dedicated test pool, we run synthetic replay + a small subset of production traffic behind a canary for validation.

Attachments: shipwright_sizing_v1.xlsx, redwood_slo_proposal_shipwright.pdf

If that looks close to what you expect, I’ll get the infra team looped and share access details.

—Naomi

Thanks Naomi — this is great and captures the call. A few clarifications from our side:

- Peak profile: we typically see sustained 150 req/sec with 30–45s bursts up to ~400 req/sec for 2–3 minutes during end-of-day processing. Average payload is ~90 tokens; occasional longer documents up to 800 tokens.
- Data residency: all inference requests must originate from our AWS account and stay within our VPC; logs can be shipped to S3 in our account.

Questions:
1) Can you confirm expected hardware footprint for the pilot (#GPUs / memory) for the dedicated pool?
2) How do you handle KV cache invalidation if templates change frequently?

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Shipwright pilot: ops constraints, SLO targets & next steps (technical notes)

Looping in quick technical readout on expected footprint and cache behavior — high level notes for the infra sync: 

1) Pilot sizing (ballpark):
- For sustained 150 req/sec (avg 90 tokens) + 3-minute spikes to 400 req/sec we recommend a 4-GPU dedicated pool (NVIDIA A40/A100 class) with autoscale headroom to add 2 GPUs for spikes. That supports batching and KV caching while keeping p95 latency within target.
- Quantized 3B model should hit ~60–90ms median and p95 ~120–150ms depending on batch window. If most payloads are 90 tokens, expect lower tail latency; 800-token jobs will increase tail and should be routed to a separate larger instance group.

2) KV cache & template invalidation:
- We recommend prefix-based KV keys with a TTL aligned to your template update cadence (default 24h).
- For immediate invalidation we offer a blocking invalidation API; Redwood Console will surface invalidation events and can audit them to your S3/Audit logging.

3) Security/compliance notes:
- Private control plane + customer VPC peering keeps inference ingress in your account.
- We’ll provide SOC2 + subprocessors list ahead of the pilot; the pilot can also run in an on-prem box if you prefer air-gapped testing.

4) Observability:
- Token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency histograms, and tracing hooks will be enabled in the pilot. We’ll bind access for your SREs to the Redwood Console with read-only views.

I’ll prepare a short ops runbook for the sync with exact autoscale settings and test plan.

—Rishi
